# Manifests are data too

By Srikanth Venugopalan, 13 May 2026. Topics: iceberg.
Canonical: https://sriv.github.io/notes/manifests-are-data-too/

> Iceberg's manifests have always been row-oriented Avro. The draft version 4 spec makes them Parquet. Everything I'd learned about not reading data turned out to apply to metadata as well.

This year I moved down a layer. After two years inside query engines, deciding what not to read, I started working on the table format underneath them: [Apache Iceberg](https://iceberg.apache.org/), and specifically the metadata changes going into version 4 of its spec.

The first piece I implemented was the smallest-sounding one: writing **manifests** as Parquet instead of Avro. At the time it was a proposal under discussion upstream. It has since been merged into the v4 draft of the spec, which hasn't been formally adopted yet. This post is about why such a dull-sounding change matters, and why it helped commits as well as queries.

## What a manifest is, and who reads it

An Iceberg manifest is a list of files. Each entry describes one data file: its path, partition values, row count, and statistics for its columns (lower and upper bounds, null counts and so on).

Two kinds of readers open manifests:

- **Query planning** reads them to decide which data files a query needs, using the partition values and column bounds. This is the pruning ladder from [the cheapest row is the one you never read](https://sriv.github.io/notes/the-cheapest-row-is-the-one-you-never-read/), one level up.
- **Commits** read them too, which is easy to forget. A compaction has to confirm the files it's replacing are still in the table. A retried commit has to look at what changed underneath it. A delete or overwrite needs the record counts of the files it removes, for the snapshot summary.

In versions 1 to 3, a manifest is an Avro file, which stores data row by row. To get any field of an entry, you still have to read through the whole entry, because there's no way to jump straight to one field.

## Where Avro hurts

The column statistics are where it shows. In v1–v3 each entry stores them as maps from column ID to a value: one map for lower bounds, one for upper bounds, more for null counts, value counts and sizes. The bounds are stored as bytes, which the reader then has to decode according to each column's type.

Picture a wide table with a few hundred columns and a query that filters on one of them. Every manifest entry carries bound maps for every column that has metrics enabled, which by default is the first hundred, and planning decodes all of it to find the one pair of bounds it needs. Most of the bytes read during planning belong to columns the query never mentions.

It's the same problem as reading rows you don't need, just in metadata instead of data. And the fix is the same one.

## Parquet manifests

In v4, manifests are Parquet files. The statistics change shape too. Instead of maps of bytes, each table column gets its own typed struct inside a `content_stats` field. A column's bounds are stored as that column's real type, so an `int` column has `int` bounds.

Each stats struct gets a fixed block of 200 field IDs, starting at `10_000 + 200 × field-id`. That leaves room for every metric a column can have, including nested ones like geospatial bounds. A reader that wants the bounds for column 2 knows exactly which Parquet columns hold them, without looking at anything else.

[Diagram: An Avro manifest stores each file entry as a row, with column statistics in maps over every column, so finding one column's bounds decodes every entry in full. A Parquet manifest stores each field as a column, so a filter on c2 reads only the path column and c2's typed statistics. Commits benefit too, since they read narrow slices such as paths, statuses and counts.]

*Same manifest, two layouts. Planning and commits both want a few columns of it, not all of it.*

That buys three things:

- **Projection.** Planning reads only the stats columns for the columns in the filter, plus the path. The rest of the manifest stays on disk.
- **No per-type byte parsing.** Bounds come out as typed values, already in the right representation.
- **Pruning inside metadata.** A Parquet manifest has its own row-group statistics. A large manifest whose entries are clustered, for example by partition, can skip whole chunks of them before decoding, using the same min/max machinery we use on data.

## Why commits got cheaper

The query-side win is the obvious one. The commit-side win surprised me more.

Most of what a commit reads from existing manifests is narrow. Validating a compaction mostly needs paths and statuses. Rebasing a retry needs to know which entries changed. Updating the summary needs the record counts of removed files. With Avro, each of those still decoded whole entries, statistics maps included. With Parquet, each reads the one or two columns it needs.

Writing got better too. Manifest columns are very repetitive (long, similar file paths, the same partition values, similar row counts), and columnar encoding and compression handle that far better than compressing blocks of whole rows, which is what Avro does. Smaller manifests are cheaper to write, upload and read back on the next commit.

A commit is a chain of small reads and writes against object storage, and every one of them sits inside the window where another writer can beat you to it. Making each step touch fewer bytes makes the window shorter, and a shorter window means fewer retries.

## What it costs

Parquet isn't free, and it's worth being honest about where it loses:

- **Tiny files pay a fixed tax.** A Parquet file has a footer, a schema and per-column overhead. A manifest with three entries can come out bigger in Parquet than in Avro.
- **The schema depends on the table.** Because `content_stats` has one struct per table column, the manifest schema is built from the table schema. Schema evolution has to be handled carefully, which is why the spec says stats are resolved by ID and names are informational only.
- **Readers have to change.** Every engine that reads manifests needs a Parquet path. While the proposal was still being discussed, I kept the new format behind a switch, so tables could be moved over deliberately rather than all at once.

## What I'd tell someone implementing it

- **Treat metadata as data.** Everything you know about columnar layout, projection and pruning applies. It's easy to forget, because metadata files feel small, until a table has millions of them.
- **Look at the commit path, not just planning.** The reads a commit does are narrow and frequent, and they're exactly the kind columnar formats are good at.
- **Round-trip every type.** Bounds for floats (where `NaN` can never be a bound and is counted separately, and `-0.0` must sort before `+0.0` even though they compare equal), decimals, timestamps and strings all have edge cases. A test that writes and reads back every type is cheap, and it's worth writing before anything else.
- **Build ahead of a spec behind a switch.** Implementing a proposal early teaches you a lot, but the format will change before it's final, and you don't want existing tables quietly committed to your first guess.

---

# Porting an idea, not the code

By Srikanth Venugopalan, 18 December 2025. Topics: rust, datafusion, indexes.
Canonical: https://sriv.github.io/notes/porting-an-idea-not-the-code/

> Bringing dynamic indexes from a Java engine to one built on Rust and DataFusion. What carried over was a handful of rules. Almost none of the code did.

By the end of 2025 the team was building a native executor in Rust on top of [Apache DataFusion](https://datafusion.apache.org/). I'd spent a good part of the previous year on dynamic indexes in our Java engine ([the post on lazily built indexes](https://sriv.github.io/notes/let-the-queries-build-the-index/)), so in December I took on bringing them across.

I expected a translation job and got something closer to a redesign. Writing an idea a second time, in a different engine, shows you which parts of it were the idea and which parts were just how the first engine happened to be built.

## What carried over

Here's what survived the trip unchanged. None of it is code:

- **An index answers "maybe" or "no", and a wrong "no" is the only real bug.** Missing entries, failed builds and anything unexpected all mean "maybe".
- **Build lazily, from data the query was reading anyway.** No background jobs, no separate build step.
- **Key everything by file and row group.** Files in a table format don't change once written, so an entry for a given file stays true.
- **An index built from a partial view of the data must never be kept.** This was the rule that mattered most in Rust, for reasons below.

Everything else was rewritten from scratch, and it should have been. The Java implementation was shaped around the Java engine's scan operator, its threading and its caches. Translating it line by line would have brought all of that along into an engine that works differently.

## Use the host's extension points

DataFusion is built to be extended, and the most useful decision in the port was to lean on that instead of fighting it.

DataFusion already knows how to prune Parquet row groups. Given a query's filter, it builds a **pruning predicate**, then asks a statistics provider for each row group's min, max, null and row counts, and whether it could contain a given set of values and works out which row groups can't possibly match. The provider is an interface. DataFusion ships one that reads the Parquet footer, but nothing stops you from supplying your own.

So the dynamic index became exactly that: a statistics provider backed by our index store. Our code answers "what's the min and max of this column in row group 3 of this file?", "could it contain 42?", or "I don't know", and DataFusion's existing logic does the rest: `AND`, `OR`, `IN`, ranges and the common forms of negation, and anything it can't rewrite becomes "maybe". In the Java engine I'd written and tested that predicate logic myself. Here I got it for free, along with everyone else's bug fixes.

The other half was the scan itself. Rather than fork DataFusion's Parquet source, I wrapped it: our source holds the stock one and passes every call through, except opening a file, where it narrows the list of row groups to read before handing over. My first cut copied more of the stock source than it needed to. The rewrite later that day was mostly deleting those copies and passing calls through.

[Diagram: Row groups in a Parquet file pass through three checks in order: our in-memory dynamic index, the footer min/max statistics, then Parquet bloom filters. Each check removes some row groups. The rest are decoded with filters pushed down, so the output is not the whole row group, and a partial view must never become an index.]

*Cheapest check first. DataFusion does the predicate logic; the dynamic index only has to answer questions about row groups.*

The order of the checks matters. Our index lives in memory, so it goes first. The footer statistics come next, since the footer has already been read. Parquet's own bloom filters come after that, because checking them means fetching more bytes, and page-index pruning after them. Each check only sees the row groups the cheaper ones before it let through.

## The filter that moved

This is where the port taught me something about the original.

In the Java engine, the scan decoded a row group into batches and a separate filter operator dropped rows afterwards. Whatever the scan produced was the whole row group. Building an index from it was safe almost by accident, because nothing upstream had thrown rows away.

DataFusion can drop rows inside the Parquet reader itself: filter pushdown evaluates predicates while decoding, and page-index pruning skips whole pages before decoding starts. That's a real performance win, and you want it on. It also means the batches that come out of the scan are no longer the row group. They're the part of the row group the current query cared about. Build a min/max or a bloom filter from that, and you've built an index that will confidently say "no" to values that are sitting right there in the file.

In Java this rule had been met by the shape of the engine. In Rust it had to be enforced deliberately: an index is only kept when we know it was built from the whole row group, and anything less is discarded. I won't go into the mechanism here. The important part is being able to name the rule. Once you can say "never keep an index built from a partial view", a whole class of bugs becomes something you check for rather than something you stumble into.

## A simpler bloom filter

The first Rust version fed values into a bloom filter with a separate branch for each column type, and only covered a handful of types. In January I replaced it with a simpler design: hash every value to a 64-bit number first, whatever its type, and keep a bloom filter of those hashes.

That one change removed a surprising amount of code:

- **No type-specific logic.** Integers, strings, dates and decimals all go through the same filter once they're hashed.
- **Uniform size.** Every filter for a given expected row count and false-positive rate is the same size, which makes memory accounting predictable.
- **Mergeable.** Two filters of the same size and hash scheme combine with a bitwise OR, so filters built in pieces can be joined without going back to the data.

The one thing to be careful of is that the hash has to be stable and has to agree between the side that builds the filter and the side that probes it. Hash `5` as an `INT` when you build the filter, probe it with the `BIGINT` literal the query planner produced, and you get a wrong "no". It's the same bug from [the bloom filter post](https://sriv.github.io/notes/bloom-filters-at-the-scan/) in different clothes.

## What I'd tell someone porting a subsystem

- **Write down the rules before you write any code.** The list above came from asking "what would make this wrong?", not from reading the old code.
- **Look for the rules the old system enforced by accident.** They're the ones a new engine breaks quietly.
- **Prefer the host's extension points to a fork.** You inherit its correctness and its future fixes, and your own code gets smaller.
- **Expect the second version to be simpler.** If it isn't, you may be porting the first engine's shape rather than the idea.

---

# Spot instances and the query that must not die

By Srikanth Venugopalan, 5 October 2025. Topics: distributed, cloud.
Canonical: https://sriv.github.io/notes/spot-instances-and-the-query-that-must-not-die/

> Spot capacity is the cheapest compute a cloud will sell you, and it comes with a short warning before it's taken back. Deciding where in the stack to absorb that warning was the interesting part.

By the second half of 2025 spot instances were one of the bigger levers we had on cost: spare cloud capacity sold at a deep discount, on the understanding that the provider can take it back. AWS gives you a two-minute warning, sometimes earlier with a rebalance recommendation. Azure and GCP give you about thirty seconds. Then the machine is gone.

For a stateless web service that's an annoyance. For a distributed query engine it's a real problem. An executor that disappears mid-query takes with it the tasks it was running, any intermediate results it was holding, and, if it happened to be coordinating the query, the query itself.

In September and October 2025 I worked on making the engine survive that. The code was the easy half. The harder half was deciding *where* each kind of failure should be absorbed.

## The decision: where to retry

There are three obvious places to put recovery, and they behave very differently.

**Let the platform restart it.** Kubernetes notices the pod is gone and schedules a new one. This is free and it's what everything else in the cluster already does. But a new pod knows nothing about the query that was running. Restarting the executor doesn't restart the work.

**Retry the tasks.** The queue that hands out work knows which tasks went to which executor. If an executor dies, its unfinished tasks can be handed to someone else. The query keeps running and only the lost slice is redone.

**Retry the query.** Throw the whole query away and run it again from the top. Simple and correct for a read-only query that hasn't returned anything yet, but it can turn a short interruption into a much longer query.

The answer I landed on was all three, each at the level where it's cheapest, plus a fourth step that comes before any of them: use the warning.

[Diagram: Timeline of a spot interruption. On notice, the executor drains: stops taking tasks, finishes running ones and tells the queue it is terminating. Between thirty seconds and two minutes later, depending on the cloud, the machine is gone. Leftover work on a worker is retried as tasks elsewhere; if the coordinator was lost, the planner retries the query. A circuit breaker on the dead address makes critical calls fail fast and non-critical calls return nothing.]

*Absorbing a spot interruption: use the warning first, then retry at the lowest level that still has enough state.*

## First, use the warning

Even thirty seconds is a long time for an executor, and two minutes is a lot. Most scan tasks finish in seconds. So the first thing each executor got was a small detector per cloud that watches for the interruption notice: the instance metadata endpoint on AWS, Scheduled Events on Azure, the `preempted` metadata value on GCP.

When the notice arrives, the executor starts **draining**:

- it stops asking the queue for new tasks,
- it keeps working on the tasks it already has,
- it tells the queue it's terminating, so the queue knows not to count on it and can start moving anything that won't finish in time.

When it works, the interruption ends right there. The tasks in flight finish inside the window, nothing new lands on the machine, and the query never notices. The best retry is the one you don't need.

## Then, retry the tasks

When the machine goes before its work is done, the queue has to tell the difference between three states: alive, terminating (we were warned), and dead. "Dead" means it isn't answering *and* it never said it was leaving. That's the case where its incomplete tasks get retried elsewhere, for every query it was taking part in.

The retry is deliberately best-effort. Some work can't simply be replayed. If the machine was holding part of a join's hash table, or shuffle output that other tasks were waiting to read, that state is gone with it, and redoing one task doesn't bring it back. When a task-level retry can't put things right, the failure moves up a level instead of being papered over.

## Last, retry the query

The coordinator is the special case. It holds the query's plan, tracks which stages are done, and assembles the result. If the coordinating executor dies, there's no executor left that knows what the query was doing. So that case goes all the way up: the planner, which still has the original query, retries it from the top on a healthy executor.

It's the most expensive recovery and the rarest, and that's the right way round.

## Stop calling the dead

The part that needed the most care wasn't the retry logic. It was everything *around* a dead executor. Once a machine is gone, every other component that still has its address keeps trying to talk to it: status checks, result fetches, cleanup calls. Each one waits for a timeout. Multiply that by every query and every component, and a single lost executor slows the whole cluster down for minutes.

So executors got a **circuit breaker**. After a call to a dead or terminating executor fails, the circuit for that address opens and later calls fail immediately instead of waiting. We split calls into two kinds:

- **critical** calls, where the caller needs the answer, fail fast with a clear error, so the retry logic above can take over,
- **non-critical** calls, like a status poll or a cleanup, quietly return nothing.

That split mattered more than the breaker itself. The first version treated every call as critical. Within days I added the split.

One more lesson from this stretch: failure handling has a way of feeding back into itself. There was a recovery callback that, a couple of hops later, ended up triggering itself, and it only showed up during real interruptions. If your recovery path can trigger itself, it eventually will.

## What I'd tell a team running on spot

- **Use the warning before you build the retry.** Draining handles more interruptions than any retry does, and it's much simpler.
- **Recover at the lowest level that has enough state.** Tasks for workers, queries for coordinators, and the platform only for the process itself.
- **Make "terminating" a real state.** Being able to tell "warned and leaving" from "gone without a word" is what makes the rest of the logic sane.
- **Break the circuit, and decide which calls are allowed to fail quietly.** A dead machine shouldn't cost every other component a timeout.
- **Test with real interruptions.** Simulated notices are useful, but the cloud's timing is never quite what you mocked. Run it on real spot capacity before you trust it.

---

# One query, many clouds

By Srikanth Venugopalan, 3 October 2025. Topics: distributed.
Canonical: https://sriv.github.io/notes/one-query-many-clouds/

> When the data lives in more than one place, you can move the data to the query or move the query to the data. I spent a good amount of time learning what it takes to do the second.

Most query engines assume that all of their workers sit in one network, close to each other and close to the data. For a lot of organisations that stopped being true a while ago. Data lands in whichever cloud the team that produced it was using. A partner's data sits in their account, not yours. And a lot of the time the reason isn't cost or convenience at all: data residency and sovereignty rules decide which region or country the data may live in, and where it may be processed.

The usual answer is to copy everything into one place first. That works, but it costs egress on every byte, it's always a little out of date, and where residency rules apply it often isn't allowed at all.

From May to October 2025 I worked on the other answer: let a single query run across executors in more than one place, and have each part of the query run near the data it reads. Internally we called a group of executors in one location a **fleet**, and a cluster made of several fleets a **hybrid cluster**.

## The cost model changes

Inside one network, the expensive things in a distributed query are CPU, memory and shuffle. Across clouds one cost grows until it dominates: bytes that cross the boundary. They add latency, they're billed at egress rates, and they go over links you don't control.

That one fact, together with the rules about where data may go, shaped almost every decision:

- **Scans run where the data is.** Reading a table across a cloud boundary means paying for every byte the scan touches, including the ones a filter is about to throw away.
- **Reduce before you cross.** Filters, projections and partial aggregates should run on the data's side, so what crosses the boundary is already as small as the query allows.
- **The boundary has to be visible in the plan.** If the planner can't see where the expensive edge is, it can't plan around it.

## Run the work near its data

The first piece, in May, was teaching the scheduler that work has a location. Each stage of a query can carry a preference for which fleet should run it, and executors only pick up work meant for their own fleet. Scans of a table go to the fleet that's next to the table's storage.

None of this is a new idea. It's data locality, the same thing Hadoop and Spark have done for years with preferred locations and Presto-style engines do with split placement. What's different is the scale of the penalty. In a single data centre, getting locality wrong costs you a bit of network bandwidth. Across clouds it costs you money on every query. And when the data is under residency rules, locality stops being an optimisation altogether. Running the scan where the data lives is a requirement, and the planner has to treat it as a hard constraint, not a preference it can trade away when a plan looks cheaper.

## Make the boundary an operator

The second piece, from August, was the part I found most interesting. Once stages run in different fleets, data has to move between them somewhere, and it's tempting to hide that inside the existing shuffle machinery. I didn't. Crossing a fleet boundary became its own operator in the plan, a **remote exchange**, with its own statistics.

[Diagram: Two fleets in different clouds. In fleet A, the orders table is scanned, filtered and partially aggregated next to its data. Only the surviving rows pass through an explicit remote exchange operator across the cloud boundary to fleet B, where they are joined with the customers table and finally aggregated.]

*Scan where the data lives, shrink it there, and make the crossing an operator the planner can see.*

Making it explicit paid off in three ways:

- **The planner can reason about it.** It can push filters and partial aggregates below the remote exchange, and it can tell a plan with one crossing from a plan with three.
- **You can debug it.** When a hybrid query is slow, the first question is "how much crossed the boundary, and when?" The operator's own stats answer that directly.
- **It can be tested on its own.** The exchange has a clear contract (rows in on one side, the same rows out on the other), and that's much easier to test than behaviour spread across a shuffle.

## Joins across the boundary

Joins were the hardest case. When the two sides of a join live in different fleets, one side has to travel. It's the classic distributed join question with a much steeper price on the wrong answer:

- **Ship the small side.** If one input is small, build the hash table from it and send that table across, then probe it locally against the big side. This is a broadcast join, with the broadcast going over a cloud link. Where residency rules apply, the planner also has to know which side is allowed to travel at all.
- **Don't ship either side whole if you can avoid it.** Filter and project first, so the side that travels is only the columns and rows the join needs.
- **Decide with estimates, and be ready to be wrong.** Size estimates are least reliable exactly where they matter most, on filtered intermediate results. A wrong guess here isn't just slow, it's expensive.

By October, joins between fleets worked end to end. Their tests were flaky enough that one had to come out of CI while I chased it down, which brings me to the network.

## Getting packets across at all

Before any of that, executors in different clouds need to reach each other. The options all trade something:

- **Public endpoints with TLS** are simple, but every executor needs to be reachable from the internet.
- **Each cloud's own peering or VPN** works well within a cloud and less well between clouds, and every pair of providers is a different project.
- **An overlay network** gives every node a private address that works the same everywhere.

I spent part of September prototyping the third option on [WireGuard](https://www.wireguard.com/). WireGuard suits this kind of problem: it's small, it's fast, it's in the Linux kernel, and a tunnel between two machines is just a pair of keys and an endpoint. The hard parts aren't the tunnels. They're everything around them: how nodes find each other, how keys are handed out and rotated, and how two nodes that are both behind NAT reach each other at all. I'm not going to go into how I handled those, but if you're starting down this road, budget for the control plane, not the data plane.

## Where we went further

Everything above is the textbook version, and you can build it from ideas that are already public. At [e6data](https://www.e6data.com/) we didn't stop at locality. How our scheduler decides where each piece of a hybrid query runs is the part of that work I'm proudest of. It's also the part I can't write about yet. If the textbook version is hitting its limits in your own cross-cloud setup, keep an eye on what our engineering team writes up.

## What I'd tell a team going hybrid

- **Make egress the first number in your cost model.** Most of the design falls out of taking it seriously.
- **Put the boundary in the plan.** An explicit operator for "data crosses fleets here" is easier to optimise, debug and test than a property hidden in the shuffle.
- **Locality is old; the penalty is just steeper.** Reuse the ideas every distributed engine already has, and tune them for a much steeper cost of getting it wrong.
- **Expect flaky tests and treat them as signal.** Tests that span fleets fail in ways single-network tests never do. Most of the time they're telling you something true about timing and failure in a real network.

---

# Blitz: a file format for vectors on object storage

By Srikanth Venugopalan, 25 February 2025. Topics: vectors, file formats.
Canonical: https://sriv.github.io/notes/blitz-a-file-format-for-vectors/

> Vector search wants a handful of vectors out of millions, at full precision, from storage that charges you per request. None of the formats I tried did that well in my setup, so I wrote a small one that did.

[What I tried and threw away](https://sriv.github.io/notes/what-we-tried-and-threw-away/) ended with a vector database library taken back out of the engine and a decision to write my own format. Three days later, on 6 January, the first commit of **Blitz** landed. By the end of February it had the shape it kept. I talked about it at Rootconf in 2025. This is the written version, with a bit more of the reasoning.

## What the benchmarks said first

Blitz didn't start as a design. It started as a few weeks of reading and benchmarking in December, trying to answer one question before writing any code: which existing format can hand back a few specific vectors, fast, out of a large file?

The test was deliberately plain. Random 1,024-dimension float vectors, a hundred thousand of them and then a million and more, and two workloads: read everything, and fetch a thousand vectors at random. Four candidates:

- **Parquet, as usual.** Fine for reading everything at the smaller sizes, which is what it's built for.
- **Parquet, transposed**, so that each vector became its own column and could be read in one contiguous piece. Reads came out roughly sixty times slower than plain Parquet. Worse, at a million vectors neither Parquet layout I'd built could even be opened: with the row-group settings I was using, the footer outgrew the reader's limit on how large its metadata could be.
- **Lance**, which was designed with vectors in mind. Its full scans kept up with Parquet. Random fetches through the integration I had then were the slower of the two formats that still opened at a million vectors. That says more about my integration than about the format.
- **Avro**, using a sorted key-value file with an index alongside. Random fetches stayed flat from a hundred thousand vectors to two million, because the index points straight at the record. Then I varied how often the index records an entry. Going from every record to every two-thousandth record made random fetches more than a thousand times slower.

Two things from that study ended up in the format almost directly. A footer whose size depends on the wrong thing will eventually stop a file from opening. Blitz's footer grows only with the rows of its own data file, which the writer controls. And for random access, the density of the index sets how many bytes each lookup drags in: with an entry every two thousand records, every lookup reads up to two thousand records. Blitz's footer has an entry for every row.

## What the access pattern looks like

Start from what a vector query actually does. "Find the ten reviews closest to *battery dies too quickly*" means:

1. look at every candidate vector, cheaply, to work out which few are close,
2. read those few at full precision to rank them properly,
3. return ten rows.

Step 1 touches everything but needs very little of each vector. Step 3 needs very little data at all. Only step 2 needs real precision, and only for a handful of vectors.

Now put that on object storage. The cost model there is simple. Every request pays a high first-byte latency and, on the major clouds, a price. Bytes are relatively cheap once a request is in flight. A good file format for object storage keeps the number of requests small and makes each one count.

General-purpose formats are built for a different pattern: scan a lot of rows, a few columns at a time, and compress well along the way. Floating-point embeddings barely compress. Pulling ten specific vectors out of a compressed columnar file means downloading and decoding the whole pages they live in. Parquet's offset index can tell you which page holds row 48,213 and where that page starts, but not where the row itself starts, so you still fetch and decode the whole page.

## The design

Blitz has two parts, and the second one is the important one.

**The body** is just the vectors, stored as raw 32-bit floats, one after another. No compression and no encoding. A vector of *d* dimensions is exactly 4*d* bytes, so it can be read with a single ranged request of a known length.

**The footer** is the index. For every row it holds:

- the row's position in the matching data file,
- the byte offset of that row's vector in the body,
- a **binary-quantized** copy of the vector, one bit per dimension, as described in [What I tried and threw away](https://sriv.github.io/notes/what-we-tried-and-threw-away/).

The file ends with the footer's offset in its last eight bytes, much like Parquet, which keeps its footer length and a magic number there. A reader can always find its way in with one small read at the end of the file.

There's one Blitz file per data file. That's the decision from [the vectors post](https://sriv.github.io/notes/vectors-inside-a-sql-engine/) carried through: vectors stay aligned with the data they describe, so when a data file is pruned, its vectors go with it.

[Diagram: A Blitz file: a body of raw float32 vectors, a footer with each row's position, byte offset and binary-quantized bits, and an eight-byte footer offset at the end. Reading takes three steps: read the tail and footer (cached), compute Hamming distances in memory to keep the closest K, then issue ranged reads for only those K full vectors and rerank them exactly. Each file returns its own top K, merged in a final step.]

*The footer decides; the body only answers for the few rows the footer picked.*

## Reading it: two passes

Answering a nearest-neighbour query against one Blitz file goes like this:

1. **Read the footer.** One request for the tail, one for the footer. Footers are cached across queries, along with the file length, so a warm query doesn't even need those.
2. **First pass, entirely in memory.** Binary-quantize the query vector once. For each row that survived pruning and the query's filters, compute the Hamming distance between its bits in the footer and the query's bits. That's an XOR and a popcount per word. Keep the closest *K*, where *K* comes from the query's `LIMIT`, pushed down to the scan.
3. **Second pass, a few targeted reads.** Look up the byte offsets of those *K* rows. Sort the ranges, merge any that sit close together, and fetch them with parallel ranged reads. Compute the exact distance on the full-precision vectors.
4. **Merge across files.** Each file contributes its own top *K*. A final operator collects every file's candidates, already scored at full precision, and orders them into the global top *K*.

The arithmetic is what makes it work. A 1,536-dimension embedding is 6 KB at full precision and 192 bytes as bits, 32 times smaller. The first pass runs over the small copies, which already sit in memory. The second pass touches a handful of full vectors with a handful of requests. Nothing reads the whole body.

## What I'd do the same way again

**Put the index in the footer.** The decision a reader has to make comes before any expensive read, so everything needed to make it lives in one place that can be fetched and cached in one go.

**Keep the body boring.** Fixed-size, uncompressed records mean every read has an exact, known length, and there's nothing to decode. The cleverness belongs in the footer, not in the bytes on disk.

**Count requests, not bytes.** Sorting and merging nearby ranges before fetching is cheap to do, and on object storage it goes straight at the cost that matters.

**Own the small thing.** The writer and reader together are a few hundred lines. Being small enough to read in one sitting, and to debug with a hex dump, is a real feature for a format that sits on a query's critical path.

## What it doesn't do

It's worth being clear about the edges:

- **The footer grows with the row count.** Every row has an entry, so very large data files mean large footers. That's fine while footers fit comfortably in a cache, and it's the first thing I'd revisit for much larger files.
- **Recall depends on the first pass.** Binary quantization is a rough estimate. The first pass keeps exactly *K* candidates. Keeping a few multiples of *K* would trade more reads for better recall, and that knob deserves more attention than a default.
- **It's an exact-rerank design, not a graph index.** There's no HNSW-style structure here. For analytical queries that filter first and then rank, that was the right trade. For a pure similarity-search service at very large scale, it might not be.

In March Blitz picked up its own reader and writer tests and a feature flag, and it was merged to main in the summer. The next stretch of work moved from making one machine fast to making many machines cooperate.

---

# What I tried and threw away

By Srikanth Venugopalan, 3 February 2025. Topics: vectors, experiments.
Canonical: https://sriv.github.io/notes/what-we-tried-and-threw-away/

> Three experiments that didn't make it: virtual threads for the executor, a vector database library, and product quantization. Each one taught me something the successes didn't.

Engineering write-ups tend to read like a list of things that worked. This post is the other list. Between September 2024 and February 2025 I tried at least three things that never shipped in the form I first built them. I think they're worth writing down, partly because each one changed what we did next, and partly because knowing when to stop is a skill I've had to learn on purpose.

## Virtual threads for the executor

In September 2024 Java 21's virtual threads were still the new thing in the JVM world. Our executor runs a lot of concurrent work on thread pools, so the obvious experiment was to swap the pools' thread factories for virtual threads and see what happened. The change itself was small. I did it on a branch, ran it, and it never went to main.

The lesson was about what virtual threads are for. They make *blocking* cheap: a virtual thread waiting on the network or a lock gets parked and its carrier thread goes off to do something else. An executor's pipeline workers mostly aren't waiting. They're decoding Parquet pages and running vectorized operators, which is CPU work. Putting CPU-bound work on virtual threads doesn't make it faster, and it brings its own surprises: virtual threads aren't time-sliced, so long CPU-bound tasks can monopolise the carrier threads, and you lose the pool sizing you were using as back-pressure.

Virtual threads did end up in the codebase later, in exactly the place they suit: the vector loading path, where a thread spends most of its life waiting for an embedding server to reply. Same feature, different job, and that time it was the right call.

**What I took from it:** match the concurrency tool to what the threads actually spend their time doing. Profile first, then pick the tool.

## A vector database library inside the engine

When I started on vector search ([the vectors post](https://sriv.github.io/notes/vectors-inside-a-sql-engine/)), one tempting shortcut was to borrow from a project that had already solved vector storage. In December I pulled a vector database library into the executor so I could benchmark its format against Parquet and Avro for reading embeddings.

It came out again on 3 January.

That wasn't a verdict on the library. The question I was really asking was "should our engine's scan path depend on this?", and the answer was no. Taking a dependency like that into the core of a query engine means taking on its release cycle, its memory model and its idea of how files should be laid out and read. Our scan path already had strong opinions about memory and layout: per-file alignment with the table's data, our own caching, our own I/O. I'd just spent months teaching the engine to read fewer bytes, and a library that owns its own file layout would have sat outside all of that. What I needed was a format that fit those opinions, and three days after removing the library I started writing one. That's [Blitz](https://sriv.github.io/notes/blitz-a-file-format-for-vectors/).

**What I took from it:** benchmark against the best available option even when you suspect you won't adopt it. It tells you what "good" looks like, and it makes the case for building your own honestly instead of by default.

## Product quantization

The third experiment was about making brute-force vector search cheaper. Exact search reads every candidate vector at full precision. Quantization compresses vectors so the first pass reads far less.

**Product quantization** (PQ) is the classic approach. Split each vector into sub-vectors, run k-means separately on each sub-vector position, across a sample of the data, to learn a small codebook for it, and store each sub-vector as the ID of its nearest codebook entry. You get large compression and decent distance estimates.

In late January I built a PQ prototype on a branch. It never made it to main.

PQ needs **training**. The codebooks are learned from the data, so every table needs a k-means step before its vectors can be compressed, and codebooks go stale as the data changes. For a search service with one big, stable index that's a fine trade. For an engine where vectors arrive with each new data file, it's an extra build step with its own failure modes and tuning, on the critical path of every load.

A week later I tried the much blunter tool, **binary quantization**: keep one bit per dimension, its sign. It works best on high-dimensional embeddings centred around zero, and needs no training, no codebooks and nothing that goes stale. Distances become a Hamming distance, which is an XOR and a population count, about the cheapest thing a CPU can do. The estimates are much rougher than PQ's, so it can't answer a query on its own. But it doesn't need to. It's a first pass that throws away the obviously far vectors, followed by an exact rerank of the survivors at full precision.

[Diagram: Product quantization splits a vector into sub-vectors and stores codebook IDs learned with k-means; it compresses well but needs training. Binary quantization keeps only the sign of each dimension; it needs no training and uses XOR and popcount, so it serves as a rough first pass before an exact rerank.]

*Two ways to shrink a vector. The better compressor lost to the one with no training step.*

**What I took from it:** prefer the technique whose costs match the system's shape. PQ gives better distance estimates for the same number of bits. Binary quantization was better for an engine that loads data continuously and already knows how to do an exact second pass.

## On stopping

None of these were mistakes, and none of them were wasted. Each one ran for weeks at most. Each one lived on a branch, where it could fail cheaply, and each one changed the next decision: where to use virtual threads, whether to build our own vector format, which quantization to use.

The pattern I try to follow now is simple. Give an experiment a question to answer, not a feature to ship. When it has answered the question, stop, even if the answer is "no", and write down why. The writing-down part is the one I'm most tempted to skip, and it's the only thing that stops someone, often me, from running the same experiment again a year later.

---

# Vectors inside a SQL engine

By Srikanth Venugopalan, 17 December 2024. Topics: vectors.
Canonical: https://sriv.github.io/notes/vectors-inside-a-sql-engine/

> Most teams I talked to were standing up a separate vector database. I tried making similarity search just another thing our query engine could do.

At the end of 2024 every conversation about search seemed to start with "which vector database?". The usual shape was a second system next to the warehouse: copy the text out, embed it, load the vectors into a dedicated store, and join the results back to the tables in application code.

We already had an engine that was good at scanning large tables in object storage, with the indexes and pruning from [bloom filters](https://sriv.github.io/notes/bloom-filters-at-the-scan/) and [lazily built indexes](https://sriv.github.io/notes/let-the-queries-build-the-index/). In November I started on the other option: make similarity search something the SQL engine does itself, over the tables people already have.

## The decision: a column, not a database

The core choice was how a user should see vectors. There were two shapes.

**Vectors as data the user manages.** The table gets an `embedding` column of floats. The user computes embeddings somewhere, writes them in, and queries with distance functions over that column. This is flexible and simple, and it pushes the hard work back onto the user.

**Vectors as something the engine maintains for a text column.** The user says "make `review_title` searchable". The engine computes embeddings for that column and stores them next to the data. At query time the user writes something like:

```sql
SELECT review_title, rating
FROM reviews
ORDER BY cosine_distance(review_title, 'battery dies too quickly')
LIMIT 10;
```

The engine embeds the query string once, compares it against the stored vectors for `review_title`, and returns rows. The user never touches a vector.

I went with the second. A query engine's job is to hide physical layout from the person writing SQL. Making them handle 768 or 1,536 floats per row felt like the same mistake as making them pick which Parquet row groups to read. The embeddings became, in effect, a hidden column the engine owns: created by a separate `LOAD VECTOR` job rather than inside anyone's ingestion pipeline, kept beside the table's own files, and used only through functions like `cosine_distance`.

[Diagram: At load time, a text column is sent through an in-cluster embedding model and the vectors are written beside each data file. At query time, the query string is embedded once, the vectors of files that survive pruning and filters are scanned with an exact distance, and the top results are returned.]

*Embeddings are a column the engine owns. Load once; at query time, embed the question and scan what survives pruning.*

## Embeddings at load time

Computing an embedding is the expensive part, so the first question was when to do it. At query time is a non-starter: embedding every row on every query costs far more than the search. So `LOAD VECTOR` runs as its own job: scan the text column, send batches to an embedding model, write the vectors out alongside the data files they came from.

My first version called a hosted embedding API. That was enough to get the load path working end to end, and it also made the trade-offs obvious: every row of the customer's text leaves the cluster, throughput depends on someone else's rate limits, and cost scales with table size. Within a week I'd moved the load path onto a self-hosted embedding server running next to the engine. Same interface, but the model runs where the data is and the throughput is ours to scale.

The detail that mattered most was keeping vectors aligned with the files they describe. Each data file gets its own set of embeddings, so when the engine prunes a file using its indexes and statistics, it skips that file's vectors too. Similarity search inherits the scan's pruning for free, and filters like `WHERE rating < 3` cut down the work before any distance is computed.

## Brute force, on purpose

The other big decision was not to start with an approximate index.

Most vector databases lead with an approximate index, such as HNSW graphs or IVF clusters. They answer "the nearest 10 vectors" without looking at most of them, at the cost of sometimes missing a true neighbour. They're the right tool for a dedicated, latency-sensitive search service.

I started with exact search: compute the distance to every candidate vector and keep the best. Three reasons:

- **It's always right.** Exact search is the baseline you measure every approximation against. Starting there meant I'd know exactly what I gave up later.
- **It composes with SQL.** A plain approximate index answers "nearest overall". Filtered variants exist, but keeping recall up when the filter is selective is still hard. Real queries say "nearest among the reviews from last month with rating under 3". With an exact scan, the filter runs first and the distance is computed only on what's left. Combining selective filters with approximate indexes is a well-known source of quietly bad results, such as too few rows or missed neighbours.
- **An analytical engine is good at scans.** Splitting the scan across files and executors, computing distances in vectorized batches, and merging each part's best results is exactly the kind of work the engine already does well.

The cost is obvious: you read every surviving vector. That is fine when filters and pruning have already cut the candidates down, and expensive when they haven't. It set up the next two months of work: making that read as cheap as possible.

## Where to keep the vectors

The last open question in December was physical: what format should the vectors be stored in? There were three obvious candidates. Parquet, because everything else was Parquet. Avro, because it stores each vector's floats as one simple array, without Parquet's per-element list encoding. And Lance, a newer columnar format built with vectors in mind.

I wrote benchmarks to read embeddings through all three in the engine's own scan path. [What I tried and threw away](https://sriv.github.io/notes/what-we-tried-and-threw-away/) covers why I didn't adopt any of them, and how that led to writing my own format in January.

## What I'd tell a team starting on this

- **Decide who owns the embeddings.** If users own them, you've built a distance function. If the engine owns them, you've built a feature. The second is more work and much more useful.
- **Start exact.** Get exact search right, with filters, before adding anything approximate. You'll need it as the reference anyway.
- **Align vectors with data files.** Then every pruning trick you already have applies to vector search without extra work.

---

# Let the queries build the index

By Srikanth Venugopalan, 4 December 2024. Topics: indexes.
Canonical: https://sriv.github.io/notes/let-the-queries-build-the-index/

> Most Parquet files don't carry bloom filters, and we didn't control the writers. So the engine started building its own indexes from data it was reading anyway.

[The bloom filter post](https://sriv.github.io/notes/bloom-filters-at-the-scan/) ended on an awkward fact. Bloom filter pruning works well when the Parquet file has bloom filters, and most files don't. Writers leave them off by default, and in a lakehouse the engine reading the table often isn't the system that wrote it.

So the question for the rest of 2024 was: if the files won't carry the index, can the engine build it?

## The decision: build it lazily

There were two ways to go about it.

**A background indexer.** A separate job walks the tables, reads the data, builds bloom filters or range indexes for chosen columns, and stores them. Queries find the index ready and waiting.

**Build it as a side effect of queries.** When a scan reads a column that's used in an equality filter, it has the values in hand anyway. Feed them into a bloom filter as the batch goes past, and store that filter for the next query.

The background indexer is the more conventional design, and it gives predictable query times. But it has to decide what to index before anyone asks, and unless something tells it otherwise, it spends compute on tables nobody queries. It also needs its own scheduling, its own failure handling, and something to tell it which columns matter.

The lazy approach gets the "which columns" question answered for free: the queries tell you. The first query against a file pays a small indexing cost on top of a read it was doing anyway. Every later query with a filter on that column can skip row groups. Tables nobody queries never get indexed. And there's no new service to run.

I went with lazy. The price is that the first query isn't faster, only the ones after it, and that the engine is now writing state it will later trust to skip data. The rule from [the cheapest row](https://sriv.github.io/notes/the-cheapest-row-is-the-one-you-never-read/), "maybe, never a wrong no", stops being a property of Parquet and becomes our problem.

[Diagram: A query's scan builds a transient filter. If the task saw every row it commits the filter to the index store; if it failed, was cancelled or stopped at a LIMIT, the filter is thrown away. Later queries use the store to skip row groups. Indexes are persisted to object storage and loaded back in the background after a restart.]

*The life of a lazily built index. The only path into the store goes through "saw every row".*

## Where a lazily built index can lie

Building the filter is easy. Building one that never gives a wrong "no" took most of the work, and almost all of it came down to one question: did this task see *every* row of the row group it's about to vouch for?

Some ways the answer can quietly be "no":

- **The task fails partway.** Half a file's values went into the filter, then the executor ran out of memory. That's what the commit and rollback from the bloom filter post were for. Nothing becomes visible until the task finishes the file cleanly, and a failed task throws its transient filters away.
- **The query stops early.** This is the one I'm glad I caught. A query with a `LIMIT` can stop reading a file as soon as it has enough rows. Its filter would only contain the values it happened to read before stopping, and a later query looking for a value further down the file would be told "no". So scans that can stop early don't build indexes at all.
- **Two tasks index the same file at once.** Both could build a filter and both try to commit. I made registration first-writer-wins, and only the task that registered a file builds its index, so a slower duplicate can't overwrite a finished one.
- **The batch was already filtered.** If anything removes rows before the builder sees them, say a cheap predicate pushed into the reader, the filter only knows about the survivors. A later query asking for one of the removed values gets a "no". The builder has to see rows before any predicate, or any delete file, touches them. This one comes back [when the reader underneath changed](https://sriv.github.io/notes/porting-an-idea-not-the-code/).
- **The column isn't what its name says.** Tables get columns renamed, and Delta tables can map logical column names to different physical ones. An index keyed on the name a query uses can end up describing the wrong data. I fixed this for mapped columns in August by keying on the physical column.
- **The filter is sized wrong.** A bloom filter is sized for an expected number of distinct values. Guess too low and it fills up and starts saying "maybe" to everything. That's not a correctness bug, but it quietly turns the feature off. Getting the expected number of distinct values right was an early fix.

None of these are exotic. They're the normal life of a scan task in a distributed engine. That's the point: an index built inside the query path inherits every way a query can end badly, and each one needs an answer before you trust the index to skip data.

## Indexing expressions, not just columns

Users don't always filter on a raw column. A common pattern is something like `WHERE SUBSTRING(order_ref, 1, 4) = 'EU01'`, or a `CAST` of a string column to a date. A bloom filter on `order_ref` can't answer that, because the stored values aren't the values being compared.

In August I extended dynamic indexes to expressions. The scan evaluates the expression, `CAST` or a nested `CAST(SUBSTRING(...))`, on the batch it's already reading, and puts the *results* into the filter. The tricky bit is the key. Two queries that cast the same column to different types must not share an index. So the index key includes the expression itself, the function, its arguments and the target type, not just the column name.

This went in behind its own flag. Expression indexes are more useful and more dangerous than column indexes, and I wanted to turn them on separately.

## Making it survive a restart

By October the indexes were useful enough that losing them hurt. Executors restart: deploys, spot reclamation, scaling down. Each restart threw away every index and put the next round of queries back on full scans.

So I made them persistent:

- indexes are written to object storage, starting with the range indexes, alongside metadata about which file and row group they cover,
- on startup, an executor **bootstraps** its indexes in the background rather than blocking startup on them,
- until an index is loaded, lookups return "maybe", the same as if it didn't exist.

That last point is the bloom filter post's default doing its job again. A slow or failed index load can't make a query wrong, only temporarily slower. The load has a timeout so one stuck read can't hold up the rest.

The in-memory store also needed a budget. Bloom filters for a big table add up. I made the store bounded, by entry count or by memory, switchable per deployment, so the index store can't grow until it takes an executor down. A colleague later added a guard that decides whether to index at all based on table size.

## What I'd tell a team starting on this

- **Decide who pays.** Lazy indexing makes the first query pay and rewards the rest. Make that trade on purpose, and write it down, because someone will eventually ask why the first query after a deploy is slow.
- **List every way a scan can end early or partially.** Failure, cancellation, `LIMIT`, sampling, retries. Each one is a way to commit an incomplete index. If your engine adds a new one later, it needs an answer too.
- **Every new kind of index gets its own switch.** Column indexes, expression indexes and persistence each went in behind their own flag, off by default. Shipping them separately meant a problem in one never forced us to turn off the others.
- **Build the debugging tools early.** By December I could dump the index metadata and write an executor's index to object storage on demand. When someone asks "why didn't this query prune?", being able to look at the index beats guessing.

By the end of the year the engine had indexes that it built itself, that survived restarts, and that we trusted. Around the same time a very different kind of column was arriving: vectors. That's [vectors inside a SQL engine](https://sriv.github.io/notes/vectors-inside-a-sql-engine/).

---

# Bloom filters at the scan

By Srikanth Venugopalan, 20 July 2024. Topics: parquet, indexes.
Canonical: https://sriv.github.io/notes/bloom-filters-at-the-scan/

> Parquet already knows how to say \"this value isn't here\". Getting an engine to ask cheaply, and to never trust a wrong answer, was the actual work.

[The cheapest row is the one you never read](https://sriv.github.io/notes/the-cheapest-row-is-the-one-you-never-read/) ended on point lookups: `WHERE order_id = 42` on a big table, where min/max statistics are useless because the IDs aren't clustered and every row group spans nearly the whole range. In July 2024 that was the first thing I went after.

Parquet has an answer to this built in. A writer can store a **bloom filter** for a column in each row group. Ask it "could 42 be in this row group?" and it says either "no" or "maybe". If it says no, it's right. If it says maybe, the value might be there. For a row group that doesn't contain it, the filter says maybe only at its false-positive rate, often set around 1%, and then you pay for a read that finds nothing.

That's exactly the "maybe, never a wrong no" shape from [the cheapest row](https://sriv.github.io/notes/the-cheapest-row-is-the-one-you-never-read/). On paper, the job was small: read the bloom filter, ask it, skip the row group on a "no". The bloom filter turned out to be the easy part.

## Where the check goes

The first decision was where in the scan to ask the question. There are two natural places.

**Per row group, inside the reader.** The reader has the footer, so it knows where each row group's bloom filter lives. Before fetching a row group's column chunks, read the bloom for the filter column, test the value, skip on "no". This is simple and local, and it saves the expensive part: the column chunk fetch, decompression and decode.

**Per file, before the task is handed out.** If every row group in a file says "no", the whole file can go. Doing that before the scan task is created saves even more: no task and no column data fetched. But it still needs the footer and the bloom filters, so it only pays once they're cached where the planning happens.

[Diagram: Each row group's bloom filter answers no or maybe for order_id = 42. "No" row groups are skipped; "maybe" row groups are read, sometimes for nothing. Bloom filters are cached in an index store where a missing entry means maybe.]

*Asking each row group's bloom filter before fetching its data. A "no" is final; a "maybe" costs a read.*

I did the first one first, because it was self-contained and easy to test, and then added the second one in the file-pruning step once the first was trustworthy. The two share everything except where they sit. That turned out to matter more than which one was "right", because the piece they share became the most important part of the design.

## The bloom filter is a network read

Here's what the paper version leaves out. On object storage, reading the bloom filter is itself a remote read. It's small, from a few kilobytes up to around a megabyte per column per row group, but it is still a GET with its own latency. For a file with many row groups, asking every bloom filter on every query can cost a noticeable fraction of what you were trying to save.

I spent a while on this, including reading the bloom filters as one batch of vectored ranges instead of one after another. Batching helped, but the real fix was not to read them again at all. Data files in an Iceberg or Delta table are immutable: a path, once written, never changes, and compaction writes new files rather than rewriting old ones. So a bloom filter read once is good for as long as the file exists. (Plain directory-based tables can rewrite a file in place, which is a good reason to put the file's size or modification time into the cache key as well.)

So I put a cache in front of the reader: in-process, keyed by file, row group and column, holding the bloom filters already read. I called it the **index store**, because I already suspected it would end up holding more than Parquet's own filters. The first query against a file pays for the bloom reads. Every query after that asks the cache.

The store also has a default that I think is the most important line in the whole feature. If a lookup finds no entry for a key, it doesn't go and fetch one. The answer is "maybe". A missing index never prunes anything. It just means you read the data, the same as before the feature existed.

## A bug that proved the default

That default earned its keep within a week. I found that the code registering a bloom filter and the code looking it up built the file path slightly differently, so lookups missed. Every miss returned "maybe", every affected row group was read, and the results stayed correct. The only symptom was that pruning didn't prune.

That's the failure mode you want. A cache-key bug in a pruning structure should cost you performance, never correctness. If the default had been "not found means not present", the same one-line bug would have silently dropped rows from query results, and we might not have noticed for a long time. The fix was a few characters. The lesson was to design the store so that every kind of mistake falls on the slow side.

## Committing an index, not just caching one

The other thing the store needed was a lifecycle. A scan task can fail halfway: the executor is under memory pressure, a read times out, the task gets cancelled. If the reader has registered half of a file's bloom filters by then, what state is the store in?

For bloom filters read straight from Parquet this is mostly harmless, since each filter is complete on its own. But I already knew where this was heading. The next step was going to be indexes the engine builds for itself while scanning, and a half-built index is exactly the kind of structure that can give a wrong "no".

So entries in the store got a **commit and rollback**:

- while a task is reading, any index it builds is transient and invisible to other queries,
- when the task finishes reading the file cleanly, it commits, and the entries become visible,
- if the task fails or is cancelled, it rolls back, and the transient entries are dropped.

It looks like a lot of ceremony for a cache. It's the part of this work I'm happiest I did early, because everything that came after depends on it.

## What I'd do the same way again

Two things from that month that I still apply:

- **Make "unknown" the safe answer.** Any structure that can skip work should treat missing or broken metadata as "read it". Then bugs show up in latency graphs rather than in someone's quarterly numbers.
- **Price the metadata read.** On object storage, metadata isn't free. Cache anything immutable, and measure how much time goes into asking the index before celebrating what the index saves.

There was one more lesson that set up what came next. Most of the Parquet files we met didn't have bloom filters at all. Common writers leave them off by default, and you rarely control the writer. If we wanted bloom-filter pruning on the tables people actually had, the engine would have to build the filters itself, from the data it was already reading.

That's [letting the queries build the index](https://sriv.github.io/notes/let-the-queries-build-the-index/).

---

# The cheapest row is the one you never read

By Srikanth Venugopalan, 31 May 2024. Topics: engines, pruning.
Canonical: https://sriv.github.io/notes/the-cheapest-row-is-the-one-you-never-read/

> Before indexes, vectors or distributed anything, I had to learn where our query engine actually spent its time. The answer: reading things it didn't need.

At the end of May 2024 I moved onto the execution side of our query engine. It's a pipelined, vectorized engine written in Java that runs SQL over Parquet files sitting in object storage. I'd used engines like this for years. I had never had to make one faster.

My instinct was to go looking for a slow operator, a join that spilled or an aggregation that hashed badly. So I spent the first couple of weeks with a profiler and a set of slow queries, and the profiles kept telling me something else. The joins and aggregations weren't where the time went. It went into getting bytes off object storage, decompressing them, and turning them into column vectors, often for rows that a filter would throw away two operators later.

That changed how I thought about the next two years of work, so it seems like the right place to start these notes.

## How a query actually runs

The planner turns SQL into a tree of physical operators: scan, filter, project, join, aggregate. The executor cuts that tree into **pipelines**, chains of operators that can pass data along without waiting. A pipeline ends wherever an operator has to see all of its input before it can produce anything. Building the hash table for a join is one of those points. Sorting is another.

Data moves through a pipeline in **batches**. Each batch is a set of column vectors, a few thousand rows per column, and each operator works on a whole batch at a time instead of row by row. That's the "vectorized" part, and it's why these engines are fast once the data is in memory.

[Diagram: The six steps of a Parquet scan on object storage. The later a row is rejected, the more it has already cost.]

*The scan, top to bottom. Every step down is more work spent on rows the filter may throw away.*

The scan sits at the bottom of every leaf pipeline, and on a lakehouse it does a lot more than "read a file". For a Parquet file on S3 it has to:

1. work out which files belong to the query (table metadata, partitions),
2. read each file's footer to find the row groups and column chunks,
3. fetch the column chunks it needs, as ranged GETs over the network,
4. decompress the pages,
5. decode them into vectors,
6. and only then hand them to a filter that might drop 99% of the rows.

Every step costs something, and the cost compounds. A row you reject at step 1 cost you almost nothing. A row you reject at step 6 cost you a network round trip, a decompression and a decode, and you got nothing for it.

## The ladder of skipping

Once you see the scan this way, the question changes from "how do I make the filter faster?" to "how early can I find out that I don't need this data?" Engines answer it with a ladder of increasingly fine-grained checks:

- **Partition pruning.** If the table is partitioned by day and the query asks for one day, skip every other day. Free, but only helps queries that filter on the partition column.
- **File and row-group statistics.** Iceberg manifests and the Delta log keep min/max values per column per file, and Parquet writers usually store them per column per row group. If the query wants `amount > 1000` and a row group's max is 400, skip it without reading a byte of data.
- **Page-level indexes.** The same idea, one level down.
- **Late materialization.** Read and filter the predicate column first, then fetch the other columns only for the rows that survived.

Each rung is cheaper than the one below it, and each one is useless for some query shape. Min/max statistics are the clearest example. They work beautifully on columns where values cluster, like timestamps in an append-only table. They do almost nothing for a column like `user_id` or a UUID, where values arrive in no particular order and every row group ends up with a spread from the smallest to the largest. The min is small, the max is large, and every row group "might" contain the value you're looking for.

A lot of real queries are exactly that shape: find this customer, this order, this session. Point lookups on high-cardinality columns that the table isn't sorted or clustered by are where min/max pruning falls over and where the engine ends up reading close to the whole table to return a handful of rows.

## The decision: skip before you speed up

So the first real call I had to make was where to spend effort. There were two options:

- make the hot path faster: better decoding, fewer copies, smarter vector layouts,
- make the hot path run less often, by giving the scan more ways to say "not this file" or "not this row group".

The first one is the more satisfying engineering. It is also capped. A 2x faster decoder is a great result, and it still decodes every row you didn't need.

The second one isn't capped in the same way. If a lookup goes from reading 2,000 row groups to reading 3, no decoder optimization competes with that. I decided to spend most of my time on the second, and the other notes here are about what that turned into: bloom filters at the scan, then indexes the engine builds for itself from the queries it runs.

The trade-off is that every skipping structure you add is something else to build, store, keep fresh and trust. Which brings me to the rule I kept coming back to.

## The one rule: maybe, never a wrong no

A pruning structure is allowed to be imprecise in one direction only. It can say "this row group *might* have matching rows" when it doesn't. That costs you a wasted read, nothing more. It must never say "this row group has no matching rows" when it does, because then the query silently returns the wrong answer.

Bloom filters fit this naturally. A bloom filter gives false positives but no false negatives. Min/max statistics fit it too, as long as they're computed correctly. Where it gets dangerous is anything the engine builds or caches for itself, because now the engine is responsible for keeping that structure in step with the data. An index that says "no" about data it never saw is the worst kind of database bug: nothing crashes, the numbers are just wrong.

Every design in the other notes had to survive that rule first and be fast second.

## What I'd tell someone starting on this

Measure bytes, not just time. For each slow query, look at how many bytes the scan fetched against how many bytes the final result actually depended on. That ratio tells you whether you have a compute problem or a "reading things you didn't need" problem. In my experience it's usually the second one, and that's the cheaper one to fix.
